A prize is something desirable that you get as a result of winning, competing, or being exceptionally lucky or skilled. It is something that doesn't just come to you freely — there is an element of earning it, winning it, or capturing it.
Meaning 1 — Something Won in a Competition or Contest

This is the most common and familiar meaning. A prize is the reward given to the winner (or sometimes runners-up) of a competition, contest, race, game, lottery, quiz, or any other event where people compete.

The prize can take many forms:

  • Money — "The chess tournament offers a prize of ₹5 lakh to the winner."
  • A physical object — a trophy, a medal, a certificate, a car, a gadget.
  • An experience — a vacation, tickets to an event.

The key idea is that the prize is given specifically because someone won or performed exceptionally well. It is not given out of generosity alone — it is earned through performance.

Examples:

  • "She trained for months and finally won the first prize at the national dance competition."
  • "The prize for guessing the correct number was a brand-new bicycle."
  • "He entered the lucky draw and walked away with the top prize — a trip to Europe."

Notice that a prize can be awarded in a skill-based competition (like a debate or a race) or a luck-based one (like a lottery or a raffle). Both are valid uses. What unites them is the idea of something awarded to someone who "wins."

Important nuance — grades of prizes:
Competitions often have more than one prize. The best performance wins the first prize (also called the top prize or grand prize), and lesser performances may win second prize, third prize, and so on. At the very bottom, a booby prize is a humorous, mock award given to the person who performed worst — it's meant as a joke, not a real honor.

Named, prestigious prizes:
Some prizes are so famous they have become institutions in themselves. These are formal prizes given annually or periodically to honor outstanding achievement in a field:

  • The Nobel Prize — awarded for exceptional contributions to science, literature, or peace.
  • The Pulitzer Prize — awarded for excellence in journalism and literature.
  • The Booker Prize — awarded for the best novel written in English.

These are still "prizes" in the same sense — they are awarded because someone won recognition through their outstanding work.
Meaning 2 — Something (or Someone) of Exceptional Value or Desirability

Outside of formal competitions, "prize" is also used as a noun to refer to anything — or anyone — considered extremely valuable, rare, desirable, or worth having. Here, the idea of a competition is gone, but the idea of something being especially worth having remains.

Examples:

  • "That antique vase is a real prize — you won't find another like it anywhere."
  • "Investors consider that startup a prize acquisition."
  • "In the job market, a candidate fluent in four languages is quite a prize."
  • "He finally found the painting he had been hunting for years — a genuine prize."

In this sense, calling something a "prize" means it is not ordinary. It is something that stands out, something that people would compete to have if they could. The word carries a feeling of "this is special, this is rare, this deserves to be celebrated."

This meaning is also used for people. If someone refers to another person as "a prize," they typically mean that person is exceptionally talented, attractive, accomplished, or desirable in some way — someone others would be lucky to have as a partner, employee, or friend.
Meaning 3 — A Captured Ship or Cargo (Nautical / Historical Use)

This is a more specialized, historical meaning. In naval warfare and piracy, a prize refers to an enemy ship, vessel, or its cargo that has been captured at sea by an opposing force or privateer.

Examples:

  • "The warship sailed back to port with its prize — a captured merchant vessel loaded with silk and spices."
  • "Pirates in the 17th century grew rich from the prizes they seized in the Caribbean."

This meaning is rarely used in everyday modern conversation, but you will encounter it in historical texts, novels set at sea, or discussions of naval history. The underlying idea is the same — something won or seized through effort and conflict.

• Prize money — The cash given to the winner of a competition. "The boxing match had prize money of $2 million."
  • Grand prize — The biggest, most valuable prize in a competition. "She won the grand prize — a fully-paid scholarship."
  • First prize / Second prize / Third prize — Rankings in a competition. "He was disappointed to take only second prize after all his hard work."
  • Booby prize — A mock award for the worst performer, given humorously. "He came in last and received the booby prize — an alarm clock shaped like a rooster."
  • No prize for guessing — A common expression meaning the answer is so obvious that there is no reward needed for figuring it out. "No prize for guessing who ate the last piece of cake."
  • The prize is yours — A way of saying you have earned or deserved something.

These words are often confused because they overlap in meaning. Here is how they differ:

Prize vs. Award
Both are given for achievement. However, an award is almost always formal and institutional — like an award at a film festival or an award given by a professional organization. A prize can be formal or informal — you can win a prize at a school quiz just as you can win the Nobel Prize. Awards emphasize recognition; prizes emphasize winning and reward. In practice, the words are often used interchangeably for formal recognition.

Prize vs. Reward
A reward is given for any helpful action, service, or achievement — it doesn't require a competition. You might get a reward for returning a lost wallet. You wouldn't call that a prize. A prize specifically involves winning something — a contest, a race, a lottery, or being the best at something.

Prize vs. Gift
A gift is freely given out of kindness, affection, or generosity. You do nothing to "earn" a gift. A prize, on the other hand, is earned — through winning, competing, or being exceptionally valuable. If someone simply hands you money because they like you, that's a gift. If they hand you money because you won a competition, that's a prize.

Prize vs. Trophy
A trophy is a type of prize — specifically a physical object (usually a cup, shield, or figurine) that symbolizes victory. All trophies are prizes, but not all prizes are trophies. A prize can be money, an experience, or an object that is not a trophy.

No matter which meaning of "prize" you encounter, one idea runs through all of them:

A prize is not ordinary. It is something set apart — won, captured, or recognized as exceptional — and therefore especially worth having.

Whether it is a gold medal, a captured ship, or a rare gem described as "a real prize," the word always signals: this is something above the rest.
